newsitem.title: HUNGARY: British Airways sees Hungarian cargo growth.
newsitem.headline: British Airways sees Hungarian cargo growth.

text.p: British Airways PLC expects its cargo traffic at Budapest Ferihegy Airport to grow at least six percent in the fiscal year ending April 1998, on the strength of increased carrying capacity and new U.S. business, the airline's Budapest office told Reuters on Friday.
"Our target for this fiscal year has been 520 tonnes," Monika Nagy, a British Airways (BA) cargo executive in Budapest, said. The airline exported and imported 490 tonnes in fiscal year 1997.
"But we now expect even more (than six percent growth) because we have a bigger plane," she added without disclosing a revised forecast.

BA, which flies twice daily including weekends between Budapest and London, upgraded on July 29 its afternoon flight from Ferihegy to a Boeing 767 from a Boeing 757, she said. The morning flight will remain a 757.
Some of the biggest new business involves shipping parts for Hungarian busmaker North American Bus Industries Rt (NABI), which assembles buses in Anniston, Alabama, United States, she said.

BA expects to carry 500-1,000 kilograms a week for NABI, normally on the 767 weekend flights to London, where the freight will be transferred onto connecting flights to Atlanta in time for the shipments to arrive by truck at the Alabama plant on Monday mornings, she said.
"Now we have an aircraft that can carry this type of cargo," Nagy said.

The after-luggage cargo capacity should average 9,500-11,000 kilograms for the 767, compared with 1,500-2,000 kilograms for the 757, she said. Sometimes the 757 has been able to take as much as 4,000 kilograms, she added.
BA also has begun carrying a variety of other cargo from Hungary, she said.

In early July, it started shipments of spare parts to Los Angeles that should average five to eight tonnes a week. Last week, it began three tonne shipments of textiles to Dallas that should average once or twice times a week.
And BA continues to attract strong business in pharmaceuticals exports to the Far East and former Soviet republics in central Asia, Nagy said.

The heaviest routes have included Sydney and Tokyo, where single shipments have topped eight tonnes, she said. Ad hoc deliveries also have been common -- via connections with cargo planes flying from Oostende, Belgium -- to the Kyrgyz capital of Bishkek and the Uzbek capital of Tashkent.
The new business is coinciding with expected changes at the end of August in cargo shipment rates, which probably will fall for U.S. routes and rise for Far East routes, she said.
"More business to the United States should bring rates down," Nagy said. "But it's hard for us to get space on flights to the Far East, so we expect to increase our rates there."
The U.S. destinations most likely to show reduced rates include Atlanta, Chicago, Dallas, Los Angeles, New York and San Francisco, she said.
